context: A local independent cinema emails organizers who previously asked about weekday group screenings. Each gets the same available dates, film, price, and booking link.
question: Within two business days of this email, would the organizer request a 48-hour hold on a screening date?

arms.deposit_on_hold: Weekday group screening: 20 seats for $240. Request a 48-hour date hold. A nonrefundable $100 deposit, credited against the total, is due when you request the hold. Reply with a date.
arms.deposit_on_confirmation: Weekday group screening: 20 seats for $240. Request a 48-hour date hold. A nonrefundable $100 deposit, credited against the total, is due when you confirm at the end of the hold. Reply with a date.

cases.evidence: A teacher is selecting between two available afternoons for 20 students. The $240 is in the activities budget. The principal can sign off tomorrow. Before sign-off, the teacher can request a free reservation and cannot commit any funds.
The school's film club has 20 confirmed attendees, an approved $250 budget and a purchasing card. The date they agreed on is available. Their usual practice is to reserve as soon as dates open.
A coordinator asked for dates before the bus contract changed. Buses can now transport this class only on Saturdays. The school has no other way to transport students.

The club pays all event costs from member contributions and has no cash on hand today. Members vote tomorrow between two available dates. The organizer usually places a free hold while collecting votes and deposits.

A society has funding for $240 and 20 seats. It will choose the venue based on whether it permits a guest speaker after the film. The organizer has asked about this once and has yet to receive an answer.
The coordinator has an approved card and a date agreed by all members, but a strict $180 total budget for the event. Member rules prohibit charging a top-up.
